paper_a.title: NeRF: Representing Scenes as Neural Radiance Fields for View Synthesis

paper_b.title: Scene Representation Networks: Continuous 3D-Structure-Aware Neural Scene Representations

metadata.description: Both papers learn an implicit MLP-based continuous 3D scene representation supervised only by 2D posed images through a differentiable renderer. They are competing frameworks for the same problem: SRN treats geometry as an implicit opaque surface located by a learned LSTM ray marcher and decoded to color by a per-pixel MLP, while NeRF treats geometry as a continuous volume density rendered by classical alpha-compositing along the entire ray. NeRF explicitly cites SRN as a baseline and shows it outperforms SRN on novel-view synthesis.

matches.explanation: Both define a continuous MLP-parameterized scene function from world coordinates. NeRF's $F_\Theta:(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{d})\to(\mathbf{c},\sigma)$ folds geometry and view-dependent color into a single 5D MLP, whereas SRN factors the same role across a feature MLP $\Phi:\mathbb{R}^3\to\mathbb{R}^n$ (DP227.2) and a per-pixel decoder MLP that produces RGB from $\mathbf{v}$ (DP227.7). SRN has no view-direction input. This is the central conceptual correspondence and the reason the pair was curated.

Both encode where matter is in the scene. NeRF's volume density $\sigma(\mathbf{x})$ (DP226.2) is a soft, differential ray-termination probability, supporting volumetric integration; SRN's surface set $\Omega$ (DP227.4) is a hard implicit level-set treated as an opaque surface. Same conceptual slot (geometry container) under fundamentally different formulations - a hallmark of CF.

Identical mathematical object: parameterization of the camera ray through a pixel given camera pose and intrinsics. NeRF writes it as $\mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}$; SRN writes the same line in world coordinates as $\mathbf{r}_{u,v}(d) = \mathbf{R}^T(\mathbf{K}^{-1}(u,v,d)^T-\mathbf{t})$, which expands NeRF's $\mathbf{o}$ and $\mathbf{d}$ from $(u,v,\mathbf{K},\mathbf{E})$. Same standard pinhole-camera ray.
Accumulated transmittance $T(t)=\exp(-\int_{t_n}^t\sigma\,ds)$ is a building block of NeRF's volume-rendering integral. SRN does not integrate along the ray and so has no transmittance-like quantity.
Sinusoidal positional encoding $\gamma(\cdot)$ is one of NeRF's distinctive contributions and has no SRN counterpart. SRN feeds raw $\mathbf{x}$ into $\Phi$ without Fourier features.

Stratified quadrature sampling is specific to NeRF's volume-integration pipeline. SRN does not numerically integrate along the ray - it walks to a single surface intersection - so there is no comparable sample-set definition.

NDC space is used by NeRF only for forward-facing real scenes (Appendix C). It is also a generic graphics primitive (origin: external) and has no analog in the SRN paper, which works directly in world coordinates.

Continuous volume-rendering integral $C(\mathbf{r}) = \int T(t)\sigma(\mathbf{r}(t))\mathbf{c}(\mathbf{r}(t),\mathbf{d})dt$ and its quadrature estimator are the engine of NeRF and have no SRN analog. SRN's renderer evaluates $\Phi$ at a single estimated surface point and pushes it through the pixel generator instead of integrating along the ray. This is the single largest mathematical divergence between the two frameworks.

Coarse-network normalized weights $\hat{w}_i = w_i/\sum_j w_j$ define an importance-sampling PDF unique to NeRF's two-pass hierarchical scheme. SRN uses no such PDF since it does not integrate along the ray.

Both papers use a squared-error photometric reconstruction loss between rendered and observed pixels as the primary supervision signal. NeRF's loss (EP226.4) sums coarse and fine network errors over a ray batch in a single scene. SRN's joint objective (EP227.2) contains the same image-MSE term plus a depth-positivity regularizer and a Gaussian latent-code prior, summed across instances and views. Same role, but SRN's loss includes additional regularizers tied to the multi-instance hypernetwork formulation.
NDC ray origin/direction formulas are NeRF-specific (Appendix C); SRN has no NDC reparameterization.

Both pose the inverse problem of learning a 3D scene representation from posed 2D images for novel-view synthesis. NeRF's problem (ProbP226.1) is single-scene: synthesize new views given posed RGB images of one scene. SRN's problem (ProbP227.2) is multi-instance: jointly learn a renderer, hypernetwork, and per-instance latent codes across a class of scenes. Same task at the per-scene level but SRN extends to discovering shape/appearance priors over a class - an axis NeRF does not target.
SRN's ray-surface intersection optimization $\arg\min\{d>0 : \mathbf{r}_{u,v}(d)\in\Omega\}$ is not posed in NeRF, which avoids surface localization entirely by integrating the volume.

Both are the top-level training algorithm: SGD on a photometric loss with a differentiable renderer in the loop. NeRF's procedure (AP226.1) trains coarse+fine MLPs for one scene with positional encoding, stratified+importance sampling, and Adam. SRN's procedure (AP227.4) jointly trains the renderer, hypernetwork, and latent codes across many scenes with depth and latent regularizers. Composite L1 match; the two procedures are structurally similar (init -> render -> photometric loss -> backprop) but differ in scene scope (single vs class) and renderer (volume integration vs LSTM ray marcher).

Both algorithms decide where along each camera ray to evaluate the scene MLP - the heart of the two frameworks' renderers. NeRF's hierarchical volume sampling (AP226.2) uses two passes (stratified coarse then inverse-CDF fine) and feeds all samples into a quadrature alpha-compositor; SRN's RM-LSTM (AP227.1) iteratively predicts a single adaptive step length at each iteration and stops at one estimated surface point. Same conceptual slot (ray traversal sampler) realized by two completely different mechanisms - the central CF axis flagged in why_related.

Composite L2-vs-L2 entry tied to the parent match AP226.2 <-> AP227.1. Both step DAGs walk a camera ray and evaluate the scene MLP at chosen positions, but the inner control flow is fundamentally different. NeRF: coarse stratified sample (ASP226.6) -> coarse network query and per-sample weights (ASP226.7) -> normalize weights to a PDF and inverse-transform sample (ASP226.8) -> fine network query and quadrature (ASP226.9). SRN: init depth and LSTM state (ASP227.1) -> for-loop body (ASP227.2): compute world coord (ASP227.3) -> query feature (ASP227.4) -> LSTM predicts step (ASP227.5) -> increment depth (ASP227.6) -> return final intersection (ASP227.7). NeRF's loop runs over samples in parallel with a closed-form weighting; SRN's loop runs over time with a recurrent state. Listed as a single composite many-to-many entry per the L2 alignment rule.
Neural Volumes (Lombardi et al. 2019) is cited only by NeRF as a baseline (origin: external); SRN does not reference it.

AP226.4 is NeRF's prose summary of paper B itself - it cites Sitzmann et al. NeurIPS 2019 (the SRN paper) and describes the scene-as-MLP plus recurrent-ray-marcher pipeline. The cited content corresponds to SRN's own joint training algorithm AP227.4 together with the RM-LSTM ray marcher AP227.1. Cross-paper external-vs-paper alignment of the same underlying method - mild evidence for the CF relationship even though it carries no information beyond confirming the pair pairing.
LLFF (Mildenhall et al. 2019) is cited only by NeRF; SRN does not reference it.
The NDC ray-space transformation proposition is a NeRF appendix result with no SRN counterpart - SRN never reparameterizes ray space.
Proof of the NDC reparameterization (PrP226.1) is paper-original to NeRF; no analog in SRN.

SRN explicitly defines the multi-instance training set $\mathcal{C}=\{(\mathcal{I}_i,\mathbf{E}_i,\mathbf{K}_i)\}$ as a first-class object (DP227.1). NeRF takes this implicitly as input to its algorithm AP226.1 but does not extract a separate definition node.

SRN factors out the abstract neural renderer $\Theta:\mathcal{X}\times\mathbb{R}^{3\times 4}\times\mathbb{R}^{3\times 3}\to\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times 3}$ as a named object. NeRF has the same conceptual mapping but absorbs it into the MLP $F_\Theta$ + volume-rendering integral and does not extract a separate renderer-as-functor definition.

The hypernetwork $\Psi:\mathbf{z}\mapsto\phi$ and the latent-manifold assumption are SRN's mechanism for generalizing across scenes in one class. NeRF is a single-scene method and has no hypernetwork or latent code - the largest SRN-side contribution with no NeRF analog.
Few-shot reconstruction objective (latent-only optimization with frozen $\theta,\psi$) is enabled by SRN's hypernetwork formulation; NeRF has no analog.
Few-shot latent-code recovery for a new instance is SRN-specific and depends on the hypernetwork prior.
